newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma says Suu Kyi breaking law, roadblocks remain.
newsitem.headline: Burma says Suu Kyi breaking law, roadblocks remain.

text.p: Burma on Sunday accused Aung San Suu Kyi and other democracy leaders of breaking laws and instigating unrest while troops manned checkpoints for the third day to prevent activists from meeting at Suu Kyi's house.

Heavily armed security police and military intelligence officers were deployed on several roads leading to the Nobel Peace laureate's University Avenue residence. They stopped vehicles and pedestrians from entering the road.

The blockades have been manned since early on Friday, when a three-day congress of the National League for Democracy (NLD) party was due to begin. Officials said the meeting was prevented because it would have instigated instability.
Police have detained about 109 activists due to attend the meeting and on Saturday held several dozen supporters who had planned to attend a regular speech outside Suu Kyi's house.
The ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council's (SLORC) actions have been condemned around the world, and Amnesty International's Indian unit on Sunday called for the release of the protesters.

"Amnesty International is alarmed that once again pro-democracy activists in Myanmar (Burma) are being detained by the military authorities to prevent them from attending a political meeting," it said from New Delhi. "These people have been arrested solely to stop them attending a peaceful meeting. They should be released immediately."
Official media said on Sunday Suu Kyi and two other NLD leaders -- Tin Oo and Kyi Maung -- had broken laws by holding weekend speeches outside Suu Kyi's house without permission.

"Daw Suu Kyi, U Tin Oo and U Kyi Maung have an attitude of opposition to the State Law and Order Restoration Council and do not abide by the existing laws and regulations," all state-run media reported.
It said government officials told the NLD in June the weekend gatherings must no longer continue.

"Despite the intimation of the officials in accordance with the law, the talks with a presence of about 2,000 to 3,000 persons continued every week," it said. "Such instigation was meant to cause disruption of stability and peace and rule of law and collapse of economic order."
In June the government passed a sweeping law prohibiting any individual or organisation from saying anything deemed disruptive to the stability of the nation.
"Of late, Daw Suu Kyi has instigated those who came to listen to her roadside talks to be courageous and defy the government without timidity," the media said on Sunday.
The weekend gatherings at Suu Kyi's house began in July 1995 after she was released from six years of house arrest.

They started as impromptu speeches to supporters who gathered at her front gates hoping for a glimpse of their leader who had not been seen for years. But the gatherings gradually grew into a regular weekly event, with crowds of up to 10,000 cheering supporters. Tin Oo and Kyi Maung also spoke on Sundays.

The SLORC has also accused Suu Kyi of working with foreign nations, especially the United States, to organise the NLD congress to coincide with the United National General Assembly and discussions on a Burma sanctions bill in the U.S. Congress.

"Theirs was a massive plot to create a political movement ... which was to have been held to cause difficulties to the government internally and to create difficult conditions to the Myanmar (Burma) government both at the United Nations and in the international communities with pressures and sanctions imposed by the Western nations," the media said.
The NLD said last week it planned the congress to celebrate the eighth anniversary of the founding of the party, which was born in 1988 after unprecedented protests against the military.
Although the NLD won a landlside victory in a 1990 election, the SLORC did not recognise the results of the poll.
